strengths: DDOME addresses a useful problem: personalizing predictions for unseen federated clients without requiring their labels or test-time fine-tuning. Selecting a small expert subset offers a practical way to limit client resource requirements.
The reported results are promising across four image and text benchmarks, including 95.7% on CIFAR10, 78.6% on CIFAR100, and 74.9% on Yahoo! Answers.

The appendices provide useful ablations of pretrained-feature quality, anchor sampling, expert initialization, overlapping label distributions, and changing client populations. These reveal meaningful operating conditions and failure cases.

The system diagram, training objectives, and pseudocode make the overall method understandable. The discussion candidly acknowledges pretrained-model dependence, communication overhead, limited scalability testing, and potential fairness effects.
weaknesses: Theorem 1's central loss lower bound is contradicted by the stated normalization. With x distributed as N(0, I_d/sqrt(d)) and unit-norm ground-truth experts, the zero predictor has loss O(log(2m)/sqrt(d)), which vanishes for m <= sqrt(d). The exact expert optimization in (1), followed by router optimization in (2), cannot have higher loss than this predictor, contradicting the claimed Omega(1) lower bound. Appendix J also changes the input covariance to I_d/d and subsequently omits covariance factors. The theoretical contribution requires a corrected statement and proof.

Even a corrected negative result for the particular random-router, expert-first procedure would not establish that joint training is generally necessary. There is no positive guarantee for joint training and no controlled experiment comparing joint and sequential training with identical features, anchors, and expert capacity.

The main specialization experiments supply substantial structure through their construction: quantity-based anchors have disjoint label groups, fixed expert assignments, and explicit expert-identity supervision for the router. This weakens the claim of discovering specialization without explicit task structure. The Dirichlet experiments help, but retain preferentially sampled anchors. Selecting anchors from an existing client population and comparing against independently trained specialists using the same information would better establish the contribution.

The comparisons do not convincingly isolate the source of the gains. Main-table FedMix uses two total experts versus DDOME's five or ten; Appendix G provides useful matched-count comparisons but only with M = K. For text, DDOME alone uses a different optimizer and learning-rate decay. Appendix B.1 explicitly identifies learning-rate mismatch as a contributor to baseline degradation, without documenting comparable tuning budgets. These issues make the broad state-of-the-art claim premature.

The relationship to mixture-based personalized federated learning is incomplete. Relevant approaches such as FedEM deserve substantive discussion and comparison. Appendix I's illustrative K-means visualization does not establish that learned mixture or clustering approaches cannot handle clients with overlapping distributions.

Important reproducibility details are missing, particularly the common experts' training data and checkpoint-generation procedure despite their decisive influence. Seed counts, the meaning of plotted uncertainty bands, and several tuning details are unspecified, and no code or checkpoint link is provided. Tables 4, 7, and 8 report best test-round accuracy without a stated validation-based checkpoint-selection protocol.

Efficiency is supported mainly by counting transmitted experts. There are no comparative communication-to-accuracy, latency, or FLOP measurements accounting for the common encoder, expert pool, and training costs. Inference requires both the common encoder and the selected expert, so sparse routing alone does not establish the claimed practical savings.
